#1 I am reading the following document about Lawvere’s ETCS:

http://www.tac.mta.ca/tac/reprints/articles/11/tr11.pdf

My question is about Theorem 6 in this document. The aim is to prove an equivalence relation is an equalizer. On page 29, the author says:

Finally we can assert our theorem (I think the a0q=a1ga_0q = a_1ga0​q=a1​g in the link is a typo.) a0q=a1qa_0q = a_1qa0​q=a1​q iff a0≡a1a_0 \equiv a_1a0​≡a1​.

And finished the proof.

That is, the author proves for every element ⟨a0,a1⟩\langle a_0,a_1\rangle⟨a0​,a1​⟩ from the terminal object 111, we have the split via the map which we want to prove to be an equalizer. But to prove the equalizer result, we need that we still have the factorization when 111 is replaced by any arbitrary object. I know that 111 is the generator in ETCS, and have trouble working out the proof that the existence of factorization for 111 implies the existence of factorization for any TTT. I tried taking the elements of TTT, and unable to construct a factorization from TTT from the factorization for its elements.

Any help, please? Thank you!

Note: If someone is reading the link above, then please note that the composition is written as: if f:A→B,g:B→Cf: A \to B,g: B\to Cf:A→B,g:B→C, then the author will write fg\mathrm{fg}fg to denote the composition of fff of ggg, rather than g∘fg \circ fg∘f.
subject: Understand a proof in Lawvere's ETCS

content: #2 Interesting question! Do I understand correctly that you are essentially asking about the statement “which clearly implies the assertion in the theorem” in the first sentence of the proof of Theorem 6? I agree with you that the intended logic is not immediately obvious. We know that the required equaliser exists by Axiom 1. What the implication in the first sentence of the proof of Theorem 6 shows is that the image of this equaliser is a subset of the image of fff; the other way around is obvious from the universal property of an equaliser. From this, it is I thimk straightforward (recalling that fff and the equaliser are monomorphisms and admit retractions), using the fact that 111 is a generator, to deduce that fff is also an equaliser. Of course this has to be made formal in ETCS, but I think that is the way the argument goes, or at least can go.
subject: Understand a proof in Lawvere's ETCS

content: #3 Thanks a lot for replying! Yes, I am asking about why does it “clearly implies the assertion in the theorem” in the first sentence of the proof of Theorem 6, and I think I get your comment before “from this”. To confirm this argument. Do you mean that the first sentence of the proof gives E⊂RE \subset RE⊂R (EEE is the equalizer) and the universal property of EEE gives R⊆ER\subseteq ER⊆E (where ⊂\subset⊂ is given as Definition 4 on page 18.) and then it remains to prove that R⊂ER\subset ER⊂E and E⊂RE\subset RE⊂R implies R≅ER\cong ER≅E? Is the final step “proving R≅ER\cong ER≅E” using the retractions and 111 is a generator? If so, I think I get it, but I think I did not use the fact the 111 is a generator to show the isomorphism. Thank you!
subject: Understand a proof in Lawvere's ETCS

content:
#4 Yes, that is the kind of thing I had in mind. One has to be a bit careful with the details though; I will give what I think is a complete proof below, and I think we do need that 111 is a generator (see step 7)), and that fff admits a retraction, but in fact do not need that eee admits a retraction.

1) By Axiom 1, an equaliser e:E→A×Ae: E \rightarrow A \times Ae:E→A×A of q∘p0q \circ p_{0}q∘p0​ and q∘p1q \circ p_{1}q∘p1​ exists.

2) By assumption (this is what it means to say that it is a subset), f:R→A×Af: R \rightarrow A \times Af:R→A×A is a monomorphism.

3) Since eee is the equaliser of q∘p0q \circ p_{0}q∘p0​ and q∘p1q \circ p_{1}q∘p1​, we have that q∘p0∘e(x)=q∘p1∘e(x)q \circ p_{0} \circ e(x) = q \circ p_{1} \circ e(x)q∘p0​∘e(x)=q∘p1​∘e(x) for every x∈Ex \in Ex∈E. It follows from the ⇒\Rightarrow⇒ direction of the first sentence of the proof of Theorem 6 that, for every x∈Ex \in Ex∈E, there is an rx∈Rr_{x} \in Rrx​∈R such that f0(rx)=p0∘e(x)f_{0}(r_{x}) = p_{0} \circ e(x)f0​(rx​)=p0​∘e(x) and f1(rx)=p1∘e(x)f_{1}(r_{x}) = p_{1} \circ e(x)f1​(rx​)=p1​∘e(x), and hence (using the universal property of a product) such that f(rx)=e(x)f(r_{x}) = e(x)f(rx​)=e(x).

4) Since qqq is the co-equaliser of f0f_{0}f0​ and f1f_{1}f1​, we have that q∘p0∘f=q∘p1∘fq \circ p_{0} \circ f = q \circ p_{1} \circ fq∘p0​∘f=q∘p1​∘f. By the universal property of eee, we deduce that there is a (unique, though we will not need this) map g:R→Eg: R \rightarrow Eg:R→E such that e∘g=fe \circ g = fe∘g=f.

5) In ETCS, we are assuming that fff admits a retraction (see after Definition 2 in Lawvere’s paper; Lawvere writes that a monomorphism is a retract, which is rather confusing terminology, since ‘retract’ must then be understood in the opposite sense to ‘retraction’, whereas I at least would consider it more natural to take those to be synonymous; anyhow, it is supposed to mean that a monomorphism is a section of some map, i.e. admits a retraction). Let us denote it by f−1f^{-1}f−1.

6) We have that e∘f−1∘e∘g=e∘f−1∘f=ee \circ f^{-1} \circ e \circ g = e \circ f^{-1} \circ f = ee∘f−1∘e∘g=e∘f−1∘f=e. By the universal property of an equaliser, we deduce that f−1∘e∘g=idf^{-1} \circ e \circ g = \mathrm{id}f−1∘e∘g=id.

7) We have that e∘g∘f−1∘e=f∘f−1∘ee \circ g \circ f^{-1} \circ e = f \circ f^{-1} \circ ee∘g∘f−1∘e=f∘f−1∘e. For any y∈Ey \in Ey∈E, we have, by 3), that f∘f−1∘e(y)=f∘f−1∘f(ry)=f(ry)=e(y)f \circ f^{-1} \circ e(y) = f \circ f^{-1} \circ f(r_{y}) = f(r_y) = e(y)f∘f−1∘e(y)=f∘f−1∘f(ry​)=f(ry​)=e(y). Since 111 is a generator, we deduce that f∘f−1∘e=ef \circ f^{-1} \circ e = ef∘f−1∘e=e, and hence that e∘g∘f−1∘e=ee \circ g \circ f^{-1} \circ e = ee∘g∘f−1∘e=e. By the universal property of an equaliser, we deduce that g∘f−1∘e=idg \circ f^{-1} \circ e = \mathrm{id}g∘f−1∘e=id.

8) We have established in 6) and 7) that ggg has f−1∘ef^{-1} \circ ef−1∘e as a two-sided inverse, and thus is an isomorphism.

9) By 8), the fact that eee is an equaliser, and the fact that e∘g=fe \circ g = fe∘g=f from 4), it follows immediately that fff is an equaliser.

If you agree that this is all fine, we should add this to the ETCS entry, I suggest, since Lawvere’s assertion that this is ‘clear’ is a bit of a stretch, in my opinion!
subject: Understand a proof in Lawvere's ETCS

content:
#5 Thank you for writting down the whole argument! Yes, I think the proof is correct. I am a bit surprised that your argument does not use the fact that eee admits a retraction though. I have written another argument in a theorem prover yesterday, which seems to me are the same to yours in spirit. I used proposition 2 on page 18, which used the fact that 111 is the generator. By proposition 2, a0q=a1q  ⟹  a0≡a1a_0q = a_1q\implies a_0\equiv a_1a0​q=a1​q⟹a0​≡a1​ implies E⊆RE\subseteq RE⊆R, and also by proposition 2, the universal property of EEE implies R⊆ER\subseteq ER⊆E, and then we only require a lemma:

For subobject a:A→X,b:B→Xa: A \to X,b: B \to Xa:A→X,b:B→X, if a⊆ba\subseteq ba⊆b and b⊆ab\subseteq ab⊆a, then A≅BA\cong BA≅B.

I expect the proof of this lemma is basically the same as your argument on step 6 and 7, but I did use both the retraction of aaa and of bbb!

And yes, adding this to the ETCS entry will be great!
subject: Understand a proof in Lawvere's ETCS

content:
#6 For the proof of the lemma, a⊂ba\subset ba⊂b implies there is an h1:A→Bh_1: A \to Bh1​:A→B such that b∘h1=ab \circ h_1 = ab∘h1​=a by definition of inclusion of subsets, b⊆ab\subseteq ab⊆a implies there is an h2:B→Ah_2:B \to Ah2​:B→A such that b=a∘h2b = a\circ h_2b=a∘h2​.

Denote a′a'a′ be the retraction of aaa and b′b'b′ the retraction of bbb, then

idA=a′∘a=a′∘b∘h1\mathrm{id}_A = a' \circ a = a' \circ b \circ h_1idA​=a′∘a=a′∘b∘h1​

But we have b=a∘h2b = a \circ h_2b=a∘h2​, so a′∘a∘h2=a′∘ba'\circ a \circ h_2 = a' \circ ba′∘a∘h2​=a′∘b, that is, h2=a′∘bh_2 = a'\circ bh2​=a′∘b.

Therefore, we conclude idA=h2∘h1\mathrm{id}_A = h_2 \circ h_1idA​=h2​∘h1​. By a symmetry argument (using b′b'b′) idB=h1∘h2\mathrm{id}_B = h_1\circ h_2idB​=h1​∘h2​, that proves the lemma.
